reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Characterised by persistent excessive daytime sleepiness that is not explained by another sleep, medical or psychiatric disorder
Night-time sleep is often long yet unrefreshing, and daytime naps tend to be long and also fail to relieve the sleepiness
Severe sleep inertia, sometimes called sleep drunkenness, causes prolonged grogginess and difficulty waking
Unlike narcolepsy there is no cataplexy, and the multiple sleep latency test usually shows fewer than two sleep-onset REM periods
Total sleep time over 24 hours may be markedly increased in some patients
Diagnosis requires objective testing with polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, after excluding sleep deprivation and other causes
Wake-promoting agents such as modafinil are commonly used, and the sleep inertia can be particularly disabling and hard to treat
reference.pathophysiology: The mechanism of idiopathic hypersomnia is unknown. Unlike narcolepsy type 1 it is not associated with loss of hypocretin (orexin) signalling. Proposed contributors include enhanced activity of endogenous substances that promote sleep or potentiate inhibitory GABA-A neurotransmission, together with disturbed regulation of the sleep-wake and circadian systems, which could explain the prolonged, deep and unrefreshing sleep with pronounced sleep inertia.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive sleep apnoea and other sleep-related breathing disorders
Hypersomnia due to a medical, psychiatric or medication cause
additionalInvestigations: Sleep diary and actigraphy over one to two weeks to exclude chronic sleep insufficiency
Overnight polysomnography to exclude other sleep disorders
Multiple sleep latency test showing a short mean sleep latency with few or no sleep-onset REM periods
Consideration of extended 24-hour sleep monitoring to document a long sleep time
Screening for depression, medication effects and other medical causes
redFlags: New severe hypersomnia with neurological signs suggesting a central lesion
Cataplexy or other features pointing to narcolepsy
Falling asleep in dangerous situations such as driving
Rapid onset or a fluctuating course suggesting a secondary cause
reference.prognosis: The disorder is usually chronic and stable, though spontaneous improvement occurs in a minority; symptoms are often only partially controlled by wake-promoting medication, and residual sleepiness and sleep inertia can substantially affect function.
pitfalls: Diagnosing before excluding chronic sleep deprivation or shift-related sleep loss
Confusing it with narcolepsy type 2 given the overlapping test findings
Underestimating the disabling impact of sleep inertia
Overlooking depression or medication as the true cause of hypersomnolence
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
